title: Of virtue
paragraphs: I find by experience that there is a great difference between the flights and surges of the soul and a settled, constant habit; and I can quite well see that there is nothing we cannot do, even to outdoing the divinity itself, as a certain man says, since it is more to make oneself impassive by one's own study and effort than to be so by natural condition; and even to join to man's frailty and weakness a god-like resolution and assurance. But these are by fits and starts; and in the lives of those heroes of the past there are sometimes miraculous impulses that seem infinitely to exceed our natural strength, yet they are only impulses. It is hard to believe that these elevated qualities can so thoroughly tincture and soak the soul of a man as to become ordinary in him, almost natural. It happens accidentally even to us, the failures and abortive sketches of men, to launch our souls, when stirred up by other people's words or examples, far beyond their usual reach; but it is a kind of passion that pushes and shakes them and in some way carries them out of themselves. Once this disturbance is over, we see how they imperceptibly droop and slack off, if not down to the very bottom, at least to the point where they are no longer the same — so much so that on every trivial occasion, the loss of a bird, the breaking of a glass, we let ourselves be moved hardly less than one of the common people. I am of the opinion that, except for order, moderation, and constancy, all things are to be done by a man who is altogether imperfect and defective. That is why, the sages say, to judge a man rightly you must mainly look into his ordinary actions, and catch him in his everyday clothes.

Pyrrho, who erected such a charming system of knowledge upon ignorance, tried, like all the others who were genuinely philosophers, to make his life match his doctrine. And because he held that the weakness of human judgment was so extreme as to be incapable of any choice or inclination, and would have it always wavering and suspended, regarding and receiving all things as indifferent, it is said that he always wore the same demeanour and countenance: if he had begun talking, he would finish what he had to say even if the person he was speaking to had walked off; if he was walking, he never stopped for any obstacle in his path, his friends watching to keep him from precipices, collisions with carts, and other such accidents; for to fear or to avoid anything would have gone against his own propositions, which stripped the senses themselves of all power of choice and certainty. Sometimes he submitted to incision and cauterising with such steadiness as never to be seen even to flinch. It is something to bring the soul to these convictions; it is more to put them into effect — and yet not impossible; but to combine them with such perseverance and constancy as to make them habitual, in attempts so remote from common usage, is almost incredible to be done. That was why, being surprised one day at home in a sharp quarrel with his sister, and reproached for breaking his own rules of indifference, he said, "What! Must this scrap of a woman also serve as evidence against my principles?" Another time, when he was seen defending himself against a dog, he said, "It is very hard wholly to put off man; and we must do our best to resist and meet things first by effects, but at least by reason and argument."

About seven or eight years ago, a peasant who is still alive, no more than two leagues from my house, who had long been tormented by his wife's jealousy, came home one day from his work, and as she greeted him with her usual scolding, fell into such a fury that with a sickle still in his hand he cut off then and there all those parts of himself that she was jealous of, and threw them in her face. And it is said that a young gentleman of our nation, lively and amorous, having by his perseverance at last softened the heart of a fair mistress, was enraged when at the point of consummation he found himself unable to perform, and that,
"Nec viriliter Iners senile penis extulit caput."

as soon as he got home he cut off the offending member and sent it to his mistress as a cruel and bloody offering in expiation of his fault. If this had been done out of considered reflection, and on religious grounds, as the priests of Cybele did, what should we say of so high an action?

A few days ago at Bergerac, five leagues from my house, up the river Dordogne, a woman who the night before had been beaten and abused by her husband, a quick-tempered ill-natured fellow, resolved to escape his ill-treatment at the cost of her life. As soon as she was up the next morning, she went, as she usually did, to visit her neighbours, and after letting fall some words to settle her affairs, she took a sister of hers by the hand and led her to the bridge. There, after a sort of jesting goodbye, without any change in her face, she threw herself headlong from the top into the river and was drowned. The most remarkable thing in this is that her resolution had been forming a whole night in her head.

It is quite another matter with the women of India. There it is the custom for men to have many wives, and for the wife who has been most loved to kill herself at her husband's death; so each of them makes it her life's work to win this privilege and gain this advantage over her companions, and the good services they render their husbands aim at no other reward than to be chosen to accompany him in death:

"Ubi mortifero jacta est fax ultima lecto, Uxorum fusis stat pia turba comis Et certamen habent lethi, quae viva sequatur Conjugium: pudor est non licuisse mori. Ardent victrices, et flammae pectora praebent, Imponuntque suis ora perusta viris."

["For when they threw the torch on the funeral bed, the pious wives with hair dishevelled, stand around striving, which, living, shall accompany her spouse; and are ashamed that they may not die; they who are preferred expose their breasts to the flame, and they lay their scorched lips on those of their husbands." — Propertius, iii. 13, 17.]

A certain author of our times reports that he has seen this custom in practice in those Eastern nations: not only the wives bury themselves with their husbands, but the slave-girls he has enjoyed as well, in this fashion. The husband being dead, the widow may, if she wishes (and few do), claim two or three months' grace to put her affairs in order. When the day comes, she mounts on horseback, dressed as finely as on her wedding day, and with a cheerful face says she is going to sleep with her husband, holding a looking-glass in her left hand and an arrow in the other. So escorted in pomp, attended by her relatives and friends and a great crowd of joyful people, she is brought at last to the public place set aside for such spectacles. This is a great square, in the middle of which is a pit full of wood, and next to it a platform with four or five steps, on which she is brought and served with a magnificent feast. After that she falls to dancing and singing, and when she thinks fit gives the order to light the fire. Once this is done, she comes down, and taking the nearest of her husband's relations by the hand, walks with him to a river close by, where she strips herself naked, and having handed her clothes and jewels to her friends, plunges into the water, as if to cleanse herself from her sins. Coming out, she wraps herself in a yellow linen cloth twenty-five ells long and, again giving her hand to her husband's kinsman, returns to the platform, where she gives a speech to the people and commends her children to them, if she has any. Between the pit and the platform a curtain is usually drawn, screening the burning furnace from her sight; some, to show greater courage, forbid this. When she has finished speaking, a woman presents her with a vessel of oil, with which she anoints her head and her whole body, and when she has done, she throws it into the fire, and in an instant flings herself in after. At once the people throw a great quantity of logs and billets on her so that she may not be long in dying, and turn all their joy into mourning. If they are persons of meaner condition, the body of the deceased is carried to the place of burial, and there set sitting, the widow kneeling before him, embracing the dead body; and they remain in this posture while the people build a wall around them, which, as soon as it reaches the woman's shoulders, one of her relations comes from behind and takes hold of her head and twists her neck. As soon as she is dead, the wall is quickly raised and closed up, and there they remain entombed.

There was in this same country something like this among their gymnosophists; for not by anyone else's compulsion nor by the rush of a sudden mood, but as an explicit profession of their order, their custom was, when they had reached a certain age or saw themselves threatened by some illness, to have a funeral pyre raised for them, with a stately bed on top, and after joyfully feasting their friends and acquaintances, to lay themselves down with such resolution that, when the fire was applied, they were not seen to stir hand or foot. In this way one of them, called Calanus, died in the presence of the whole army of Alexander the Great. And he was reckoned neither holy nor happy among them who did not destroy himself like this, sending his soul out purged and purified by the fire, after consuming everything earthly and mortal. This steady premeditation throughout the whole life is what makes the thing astonishing.

Among our other controversies, that of Fate has also slipped in; and to tie things to come, and even our own wills, to a certain and inevitable necessity, we are still resting on this argument from the past: "Since God foresees that all things will fall out as they do, which no doubt he does, then it must follow necessarily that they fall out so" — to which our masters reply: "To see something come to pass, as we do, and as God himself does (for all things being present to him, he sees rather than foresees), is not to compel the event; that is, we see because things fall out, but things do not fall out because we see; events cause knowledge, but knowledge does not cause events. What we see happen, happens; but it might have happened otherwise; and God, in the list of the causes of events which he holds in his foreknowledge, also has the ones we call accidental and voluntary, depending on the freedom he has given to our free will, and he knows that we do wrong because we have willed to."

I have seen many commanders rouse their soldiers with this fatal necessity; for if our time is fixed at a certain hour, neither the enemies' shot nor our own boldness, neither our flight nor our cowardice, can shorten or prolong our life. This is easily said, but see who is so easily persuaded. And if it is true that a strong and lively faith brings actions of its own kind along with it, certainly this faith of ours that we make so much noise about is very faint in this age of ours — unless the contempt it has for works makes it disdain their company. As to this very point, the Sire de Joinville, as credible a witness as you could ask for, tells us of the Bedouins, a nation among the Saracens with whom King St Louis dealt in the Holy Land, that they believed so firmly in their religion that the number of every man's days was set from all eternity by an unalterable decree, that they went naked to war, with nothing but a Turkish sword, and their bodies covered only with a white linen cloth; and that the worst curse they could invent when they were angry was always on their lips: "Cursed be you, like the man who arms himself for fear of death." That is a testimony of faith far beyond ours. Of the same kind too is what was given by two friars of Florence in our fathers' days. Being caught up in a learning controversy, they agreed both of them to go into the fire in the sight of the whole populace, each to verify his own argument, and everything was already prepared and the thing on the point of execution when it was interrupted by an unexpected accident.

A young Turkish lord, having performed a notable exploit in his own person within sight of both armies, that of Murad and that of Hunyadi, on the point of joining battle, was asked by Murad what, in such tender and inexperienced years (for this was his first taste of arms), had inspired him with so brave a courage. He replied that his chief tutor in valour had been a hare. "For one day," he said, "out hunting, I came on a hare in her form, and although I had a brace of excellent greyhounds with me, I thought it would be surest to use my bow, since she sat very fair. I shot at her, and shot all forty arrows that I had in my quiver, not only without hurting her, but without even startling her from her form. At last I slipped my dogs after her, but to no more purpose than the shooting had been. From which I understood that she had been kept safe by her destiny, and that neither arrows nor swords can wound without the leave of fate, which we can neither hasten nor put off." This story may serve, in passing, to show how flexible our reason is to all sorts of images.

A man of advanced years, of name, dignity, and learning, boasted to me that he had been moved to a certain very important change in his faith by a strange and odd inducement, and one in itself so inadequate that I found it much stronger as an argument the other way; he called it a miracle, and so do I, but in a different sense. The Turkish historians say that the conviction those of their nation have stamped into them, about the fated and unalterable allotment of their days, plainly serves to give them great assurance in dangers. And I know a great prince who makes very fortunate use of it, whether he really believes it or only makes it his pretext for risking himself so amazingly. Let us hope Fortune does not get tired too soon of her favour to him.
There has not happened in our memory a more admirable example of resolution than in the two men who conspired against the life of the Prince of Orange.
[The first of these was Jehan de Jaureguy, who wounded the Prince 18th March 1582; the second, by whom the Prince was killed 10th July 1584, was Balthazar Gerard.]

It is amazing how the second, who actually carried it out, could ever have been brought to undertake an attempt in which his predecessor, having tried his utmost, had had such poor success; and by the same method, with the same kind of weapons, to go and attack a lord armed with so recent a lesson in suspicion, powerful in followers and bodily strength, in his own hall, surrounded by his guards, in a city wholly devoted to him. He must have employed a very resolute arm and a courage inflamed by furious passion. A dagger is surer for striking home; but because it requires more motion and more strength of hand than a pistol, the blow is more liable to be parried or blocked. That this man was not running to certain death I do not greatly doubt, because no encouragement anyone could offer him could find any place in a sober mind, and the conduct of his exploit shows plainly enough that he had no shortage of that, any more than of courage. The motives for so powerful a persuasion may be various, for our imagination does as it pleases with itself and with us. The attempt that was made near Orléans was nothing like this; there was more of chance in it than of vigour; the wound was not mortal, if Fortune had not made it so; and to attempt to shoot from horseback, at a great distance, with the rider's body in motion from the motion of the horse, was the deed of a man who would rather miss his shot than miss saving himself. This was clear enough from what followed, for he was so stunned and stupefied by the thought of so great a deed that he completely lost his head, both for finding a way to escape and for governing his tongue. What did he need more than to ride back to his friends across the river? I have done it myself in less danger — and I think it very little risk, however wide the river may be, provided your horse has an easy way in, and you can see an easy landing on the other side according to the current. The other one, when they read out his dreadful sentence, said: "I was prepared for this in advance, and I will make you marvel at my patience."
The Assassins, a nation bordering on Phoenicia,

are reckoned among the Muslims a people of very great devotion and purity of manners. They hold that the surest way to gain Paradise is to kill someone of a different religion, which is why they have often been seen, one or two at a time, and unarmoured, to attack powerful enemies at the price of certain death, without any thought for their own danger. In this way our Raymond, Count of Tripoli, was assassinated (a word derived from their name) in the heart of his own city, during our enterprises of the Holy War; and likewise Conrad, Marquis of Montferrat — the murderers carrying themselves at their execution with great pride and glory at having performed so brave a deed.
